newsitem.title: USA: White House weighing air standards' health benefits.
newsitem.headline: White House weighing air standards' health benefits.

text.p: The Clinton administration's talks on setting stricter air quality standards centered on health benefits, not economic costs, White House economist Janet Yellen said Tuesday.
"At this stage mainly the discussion is focusing not on economic costs, but on the health benefits of alternative standards that could be set," Yellen told reporters.
"That is what most of the discussion is about is evaluating the likely health benefits --- it's a complicated matter," she said.
The Clinton administration weighed an Environmental Protection Agency proposal to set stricter air quality standards against smog and soot.

Polluting industries and areas that would not comply with the new standards said the pollution controls will cost billions of dollars, while environmentalists and health advocates said prolonging lives and improving the public's health would be larger benefits.
Environmentalists said they feared White House economists would try to torpedo the EPA proposal because of potential costs and harm to the economy.
EPA Administrator Carol Browner also has said she is bound by law to set standards to provide an adequate safety margin for public health.
Congressional Democrats were divided on the air standards issue, while Republicans lined up against the EPA plan.

At a news conference Sen. Barbara Boxer, a California Democrat, said based on a conversation last week with Browner she was optimistic the administration would adopt the EPA proposal, although with some possible changes.
The standards were a combination of variables such as concentrations of the pollution, length of time for measurement, and number of the times companies would be allowed to exceed the standards.
Also at the news conference, Rep. Dennis Kucinich, an Ohio Democrat, said he had 43 signatures of House Democrats on a letter urging the White House to adopt the EPA plan.
Rep. John Dingell, a Michigan Democrat, collected a similar number of signatures of House Democrats on a letter opposing the new standards.
